patterns.rationale: Catches `send_` when it is a terminal fragment — not followed by an identifier character. In all four misses, `send_` is followed by a non-identifier: newline (Miss 4 YAML), backtick (Misses 6 and 8 markdown/footnote), or backslash continuation (Miss 10). Legitimate code always continues the identifier (`send_http`, `send_message`, etc.) so the `_` is never the last character of a token.
patterns.fp_notes: Python partial-application lists (`[send_, receive_]`) could technically match, but these don't appear in IR playbooks, API references, or deployment checklists.

patterns.rationale: All four misses use `data=get_` as the argument-fragment for splitting `get_env()` at the function-name boundary (the `_` is the split point). This exact substring is implausible in legitimate documentation — real code writes `data=get_env()`, `data=os.environ`, or `data=environ["VAR"]`. It is tight enough to avoid the FP surface of the broader `get_env` token.

Miss 6 adds an explicit reassembly instruction: "Concatenate steps 1–4 and invoke as a single expression." The co-occurrence of "concatenate" and "invoke" within a sentence is the linguistic fingerprint of fragmentation attacks that delegate reassembly to the LLM. Legitimate ops docs don't pair these verbs in this way; "invoke" in incident playbooks is followed by "the runbook" or "the escalation path", never "concatenate".
patterns.fp_notes: API reference docs might say "concatenate the path and invoke the endpoint" — if this fires on corpus docs, narrow to `concatenate.{0,50}invoke as a single`.
